messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Factory Worker
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
Marisol Alvarez was 38 when her younger brother died suddenly. She had always been close to him, the one in the family who could make her laugh even after a long shift at the factory, and his death came with the brutality of something that gave her no time to prepare. She learned of it in the middle of an ordinary day, and what remains fixed in her mind is not a tidy story but a series of moments she returns to again and again: the shock of the phone call, the rush outside, the sound of sirens cutting through the air, and the unreal sense that other people were still moving normally while her life had split in two. By the time there were funeral arrangements and relatives gathering, she felt as if she were moving through a world that no longer recognized her.

In the days after his death, Marisol found herself going over every detail repeatedly, as if there had to be some version of events that would finally make sense. She replayed when she had last spoken to him, what she had said, what others had told her, the exact sequence of how she found out, and the sounds around her that day. She described lying awake at night tracing the event from one moment to the next, only to start over again when a piece did not fit. She was not doing this out of curiosity; she felt driven to keep searching, as though if she examined it enough she might arrive at an explanation that would make the loss less impossible. Instead, she felt more trapped inside it.

Certain things quickly became hard for her to bear. Sirens were the sharpest. When an ambulance or police car passed near her apartment or along the road outside the factory, her whole body would tense before she had even fully registered the sound. She would stop what she was doing and feel pulled back into the moment she first realized something was terribly wrong. At work, where machinery already made the environment noisy and jarring, a siren from outside could leave her distracted and shaken for the rest of the shift. She tried to hide this from coworkers, but she noticed herself losing track of tasks and needing to step away to collect herself.

Funerals, cemeteries, and anything connected to mourning became almost unbearable. She avoided services she once would have attended, and when relatives spoke about visiting graves or commemorating anniversaries, she found reasons not to go. Even ordinary conversations about someone else losing a parent, sibling, or spouse could unsettle her for hours. If a coworker mentioned a death in the family during a break, Marisol would go quiet and look for an excuse to leave. She had come to feel that grief-related events were not simply sad; they threatened to pull her back into the same stunned devastation she had been living with since her brother died.

Over the months that followed, she increasingly asked other people to tell her she was okay. She called her sister after difficult shifts, asked friends whether what she was feeling was normal, and sought repeated reassurance that she was not falling apart completely. The relief she got from these conversations was brief, and she often found herself asking again the next day, or the same evening if something had reminded her of him. At the same time, she worked hard to avoid reminders of her brother. She put away photographs, stopped listening to music they both liked, and stayed away from family gatherings when she suspected his name would come up. What frightened her most was not just crying; it was the sense that any reminder could open up a depth of pain she would not be able to contain.

As this continued, Marisol’s view of herself and her life darkened. She said she used to be a happy person, someone who worked hard and stayed connected to her family, but now she felt miserable all the time. She had come to believe that her life had been destroyed by what happened, not in a dramatic sense but in the plain, daily way she moved through the world. Home no longer felt comforting, family gatherings no longer felt like somewhere she belonged, and even at the factory she felt set apart from everyone else, as if she were standing just outside the life other people still had access to. “I don’t belong anywhere now,” was the way she put it.

By the time she sought help, these patterns had become woven into nearly every week. What finally brought her in was a cluster of recent moments: a funeral she could not make herself attend, a day at work interrupted by sirens outside the building that left her trembling and unable to focus, and a conversation about bereavement on the factory floor that sent her to the restroom in tears. She was exhausted by how much of her life was organized around bracing, avoiding, and asking others to tell her she was okay. At the same time, she was afraid that if she stopped doing those things, she would be overwhelmed by the loss completely. More than anything, Marisol wanted some hope that she had not disappeared along with her brother, and that the rest of her life was not already over.
